passage:
The doctrine of promissory estoppel has long occupied an uneasy position within contract law, and even in jurisdictions where it is firmly established, courts have struggled to determine with any consistency when detrimental reliance on a promise ought to give rise to legal relief. At its core, promissory estoppel permits a party who has reasonably relied to their detriment on an unenforceable promise to recover some measure of relief—even in the absence of the consideration that would ordinarily be required to bind a contract. The tension between this doctrine and classical contract theory is substantial, for traditional doctrine insists that only bargained-for exchanges are legally cognizable, whereas promissory estoppel appears to create obligations from the mere making of promises.

The difficulty is compounded when courts must decide the appropriate scope of the remedy. Courts in the United States have generally recognized two competing positions. Under the "expectation" approach, a promisee who has relied on a promise is entitled to damages sufficient to place her in the position she would have occupied had the promise been performed. Under the narrower "reliance" approach, the promisee recovers only the losses actually suffered as a result of relying on the promise—a measure that is almost always smaller. In a 1979 case decided by a federal circuit court, a commercial tenant had renovated premises in reliance on an oral promise by the landlord to renew the lease at a below-market rent. The court granted only reliance damages rather than expectation damages, reasoning that the absence of consideration counseled restraint and that full expectation recovery would effectively convert every gratuitous promise into an enforceable contract. The logic was that promissory estoppel should function as a safety valve for compelling cases of injustice, not as an alternative route to full contractual enforcement.

This conservative position has real merit, but its application has produced troubling inconsistencies. Courts applying the reliance measure often reach arbitrary stopping points when calculating what the promisee actually lost. Moreover, withholding expectation damages can itself produce injustice where the promisee has, in reasonable reliance, foregone other opportunities of equal or greater value than the expected benefit—yet recovery under the reliance measure does not compensate for those forgone opportunities. Commentators have noted that the purpose of the doctrine, which is to prevent injustice arising from disappointed reasonable expectations, is poorly served when the remedy is systematically smaller than the harm. One thoughtful resolution would be to permit courts to calibrate the remedy to the degree of injustice in each case, awarding expectation damages where the promisor's conduct was egregious or deliberate and confining relief to reliance damages where the promise was merely careless. Whether courts will adopt such a flexible approach remains to be seen, but the current regime—one of ad hoc determinations masked by doctrinal consistency—warrants critical reexamination.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Promissory estoppel is fundamentally incompatible with classical contract doctrine and should be abolished in favor of strict consideration requirements.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The conservative approach to promissory estoppel remedies, while coherent in theory, has produced arbitrary results in practice and merits a more flexible, case-sensitive framework.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Federal circuit courts in the United States have consistently awarded reliance damages rather than expectation damages in promissory estoppel cases.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The doctrine of promissory estoppel was created specifically to compensate commercial tenants who relied on oral promises by landlords.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Courts should always award expectation damages in promissory estoppel cases because doing otherwise perpetuates the injustice the doctrine was designed to prevent.

explanations.correct: The passage introduces promissory estoppel's tension with classical contract theory, traces the two remedial approaches and the courts' conservative preference, and closes by arguing that the conservative approach produces troubling inconsistencies that warrant a more flexible remedy calibrated to each case. B captures this full arc.
explanations.A: The passage explicitly acknowledges that promissory estoppel is 'firmly established' in many jurisdictions and does not argue for its abolition—this choice contradicts the passage's position.
explanations.B: Correct. This integrates the acknowledgment of the conservative position's merit with the author's critique of its inconsistent application and the call for a flexible alternative.
explanations.C: Too narrow—the 1979 circuit court case is a single illustrative example, and the passage does not claim that all federal courts have been consistent in this way.
explanations.D: A distortion of the illustrative example; the doctrine's core purpose (stated in paragraph 1) is general and not limited to landlord-tenant relationships.
explanations.E: Too strong—the author stops short of recommending expectation damages in all cases; the proposed solution is a calibrated, case-by-case approach, not a universal rule.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the conservative reliance-damages approach to promissory estoppel remedies can best be described as which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Enthusiastic endorsement tempered only by the difficulty of calculating reliance losses

choices.label: B
choices.text: Complete rejection on the ground that it is incompatible with the doctrine's foundational purpose

choices.label: C
choices.text: Qualified acknowledgment of its theoretical merit coupled with concern about its inconsistent and sometimes unjust application

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neutral description of a majority judicial approach without any evaluative assessment

choices.label: E
choices.text: Mild approval based on the view that expectation damages would render promissory estoppel indistinguishable from contract law

explanations.correct: The author opens paragraph 3 with 'This conservative position has real merit'—a clear concession—before cataloguing the troubling inconsistencies and the injustice it can produce. C accurately captures both the partial approval and the critical concern.
explanations.A: Overstates approval; the author's critique of the approach occupies most of paragraph 3 and is far more prominent than mere acknowledgment of a computational difficulty.
explanations.B: Too strong in the negative direction; the author explicitly grants that the conservative position 'has real merit' and does not call for abandoning it entirely.
explanations.D: The passage is clearly evaluative—the author calls the current regime one that 'warrants critical reexamination'—so a neutral-description characterization is inaccurate.
explanations.E: While the 1979 court's reasoning includes this concern, the author's own attitude is more critical of the conservative approach, not mildly approving of it on this ground.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A legal doctrine is introduced, its incompatibility with traditional theory is established, two competing judicial remedies are described and one is illustrated by a case, and the author argues that the prevailing remedial approach is inconsistent and proposes a flexible alternative.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A historical overview of promissory estoppel is provided, followed by a comparison of American and British approaches to the doctrine, and a conclusion is reached that American courts are more consistent.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A doctrinal tension is identified, three competing remedial approaches are compared in detail, a landmark case is analyzed at length, and the author endorses the expectation-damages rule without qualification.

choices.label: D
choices.text: An introduction presents a legal principle, a single case study illustrates the principle in full, and the final paragraph argues that the case was wrongly decided and should be reversed.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The passage describes the origins of promissory estoppel in Roman law, traces its migration to common law jurisdictions, and evaluates recent legislative reforms.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 introduces promissory estoppel and its tension with classical contract doctrine; paragraph 2 describes the expectation vs. reliance remedial divide and illustrates with the 1979 case; paragraph 3 concedes merit to the conservative approach but critiques its inconsistency and proposes a calibrated alternative. A tracks this structure accurately.
explanations.B: The passage does not compare American and British approaches, nor does it conclude that American courts are more consistent—it criticizes American courts' inconsistency.
explanations.C: Only two remedial approaches (not three) are compared; the 1979 case is an illustration, not an extended analysis; and the author does not endorse expectation damages without qualification.
explanations.D: The passage does not confine itself to a single case study, and it does not argue that the 1979 case should be reversed—it criticizes the broader pattern of the conservative approach.
explanations.E: The passage contains no discussion of Roman law origins or legislative reforms; it is concerned with judicial doctrine as currently applied.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, under the "expectation" approach to promissory estoppel damages, a promisee is entitled to which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Only those losses that were actually incurred as a direct result of relying on the promise

choices.label: B
choices.text: Damages calibrated to the degree of egregious conduct on the part of the promisor

choices.label: C
choices.text: Damages sufficient to place the promisee in the position she would have occupied had the promise been performed

choices.label: D
choices.text: Compensation for all opportunities the promisee foregone, regardless of whether reliance was reasonable

choices.label: E
choices.text: The full market value of any contract that the promisee entered into with a third party in reliance on the original promise

explanations.correct: Paragraph 2 states explicitly that under the expectation approach, a promisee 'is entitled to damages sufficient to place her in the position she would have occupied had the promise been performed.' C paraphrases this directly.
explanations.A: This is the definition of the reliance approach, not the expectation approach—a deliberate qualifier-swap trap.
explanations.B: This describes the author's proposed flexible remedy in paragraph 3, not the expectation approach as defined.
explanations.D: The passage limits expectation recovery to the benefit promised; it does not speak of compensating for all forgone opportunities regardless of reasonableness.
explanations.E: The passage does not discuss the value of third-party contracts; this is a plausible-sounding detail the passage never states.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that the author would agree with which one of the following statements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Promissory estoppel should be eliminated from American contract law because it undermines the consideration requirement.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A promisee who has reasonably foregone valuable opportunities in reliance on a promise may suffer harm that the reliance measure of damages fails to redress.

choices.label: C
choices.text: All courts that have adopted the reliance measure of damages have done so in order to deliberately disadvantage commercial tenants.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The expectation measure of damages is always preferable to the reliance measure in promissory estoppel cases.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Promissory estoppel doctrine is so well settled in American courts that no further doctrinal development is necessary.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 3 states that 'withholding expectation damages can itself produce injustice where the promisee has, in reasonable reliance, foregone other opportunities of equal or greater value than the expected benefit—yet recovery under the reliance measure does not compensate for those forgone opportunities.' B closely tracks this claim.
explanations.A: The author never argues for eliminating promissory estoppel; the passage treats it as an established and important safety valve.
explanations.C: No such intent is attributed to courts; the passage explains the courts' reasoning as a principled restraint rooted in the absence of consideration, not as a deliberate effort to disadvantage tenants.
explanations.D: Too strong—the author's proposed solution is a flexible, case-by-case calibration, not a categorical preference for expectation damages.
explanations.E: The opposite is true; the author calls the current regime one that 'warrants critical reexamination,' suggesting further doctrinal development is needed.

questions.questionStem: The author's discussion of the 1979 federal circuit court case in paragraph 2 serves primarily to which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Provide a concrete illustration of how the reliance-damages approach operates and the reasoning courts offer for preferring it over the expectation approach

choices.label: B
choices.text: Demonstrate that federal circuit courts have uniformly adopted the expectation approach in commercial tenant disputes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Argue that the outcome of the case was correct and that the landlord's oral promise should not have been given any legal effect

choices.label: D
choices.text: Introduce the doctrinal conflict between promissory estoppel and classical consideration theory for the first time

choices.label: E
choices.text: Show that reliance damages are always insufficient to prevent injustice in cases involving commercial real property

explanations.correct: The case is introduced immediately after defining the two competing approaches and is used to show how the reliance approach plays out in a concrete scenario, including the court's stated rationale (absence of consideration counsels restraint; full expectation recovery would convert gratuitous promises into contracts). A captures this illustrative and explanatory function.
explanations.B: The passage makes no claim about uniformity among federal circuit courts; presenting one case does not establish a universal rule, and the author's overall critique of inconsistency belies this claim.
explanations.C: The author's own attitude is critical of the conservative outcome; moreover, the passage notes that the tenant received some relief—the oral promise was given legal effect through the reliance award.
explanations.D: The doctrinal conflict between promissory estoppel and consideration theory is introduced in paragraph 1, not through the 1979 case.
explanations.E: Too sweeping—the passage does not argue that reliance damages are always insufficient; it argues that they can produce injustice in cases where forgone opportunities are not compensated.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following situations most closely conforms to the flexible remedial approach the author proposes in the final paragraph?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A court awards a promisee expectation damages after finding that the promisor knowingly and deliberately made a false promise in order to induce the promisee to abandon a lucrative competing opportunity.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A court refuses to grant any relief to a promisee because the promise was never reduced to writing, regardless of how substantially the promisee relied on it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A legislature enacts a statute requiring that all promissory estoppel claims be resolved exclusively through arbitration rather than through the court system.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A court awards expectation damages in every promissory estoppel case on the theory that the promisee's reliance is always reasonable whenever a promise is made.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A court awards reliance damages in every promissory estoppel case on the ground that uniformity in the law is more valuable than individual justice.

explanations.correct: The author proposes 'awarding expectation damages where the promisor's conduct was egregious or deliberate.' A describes precisely this scenario: a court awarding expectation damages upon finding that the promisor deliberately made a false promise to induce detrimental reliance—an egregious and deliberate act.
explanations.B: This describes a categorical refusal of relief based on a writing requirement, which is the opposite of the author's flexible, injustice-sensitive approach.
explanations.C: The proposal concerns a legislative procedural mechanism, not a remedial calibration of the kind the author envisions; it is entirely outside the scope of the proposed approach.
explanations.D: The author's approach is calibrated to the degree of injustice in each case; awarding expectation damages in every case regardless of the promisor's conduct is the uniform rule the author criticizes, not the flexible alternative proposed.
explanations.E: This describes the uniform reliance-damages approach the author critiques throughout paragraph 3; awarding reliance damages in every case prioritizing uniformity is antithetical to the author's call for flexible, case-sensitive calibration.
